newsitem.title: USA: Senate Democrats plan "targeted" capital gains cut.
newsitem.headline: Senate Democrats plan "targeted" capital gains cut.

text.p: Senate Democratic leaders plan to introduce legislation that will include "targeted" capital gains tax cuts as part of an economic growth and investment package, congressional aides said Tuesday.
Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota planned to introduce the legislation among the first set of bills from the Senate minority party leadership Jan. 21.

Daschle's spokeswoman would not comment on it, except to say the Senate Democratic leadership would introduce an investment and growth package targeted at initiatives that economists believe will help spur growth in the economy.
Another congressional aide, who requested anonymity, said, "It is intended to be a targeted package where it is targeted on the things we believe might actually result in some growth."
The package focused on small businesses, research and development, employee ownership and training, the aide said, adding that details had not been fully completed and could change.

One small business capital gains "rollover" provision would allow deferral of capital gains tax if an "original issue" of stock, not existing stock, is purchased in a qualifying small business and then sold, and within a certain timeframe the money is used to buy another qualifying small business "original issue" of stock, the aide said.
The package would take the existing capital gains preference for small businesses of assets less than $50 million and allow it for businesses with assets of $100 million, the aide said.
Also included would be a provision for companies that do a large amount of research and development investment to favour that type of investment, the aide said.

The package would allow a one-time deferral of the capital gains tax for family farms where gains were less than $250,000, as long as that money was rolled over into a qualified pension vehicle, the aide said.
A provision on individual retirement accounts (IRAs) would increase the income level that allows tax-deferred contributions to IRAs for people covered by a pension plan, the aide said.

The package also seeks to encourage companies that distribute stock options as part of their pay to do so throughout the work force, rather than just to the people at the top, and to structure it so that employees would hold onto the stock rather than cash it right away, the aide said.
The package would extend a provision, due to expire in July, to allow employees to exclude the value of training up to a certain amount a year from taxable income, the aide said.

While there were no estimates on the cost of the package, it would be in the "hundreds of millions of dollars rather than billions and billions of dollars, so it's very small in terms of its budget consequences," the aide said.
